newsitem.title: USA: Milwaukee stadium bill not needed - official.
newsitem.headline: Milwaukee stadium bill not needed - official.

text.p: A bill aimed at limiting the amount of tax revenues used to help finance a $250 million ballpark for the Milwaukee Brewers baseball team would be unnecessary and counterproductive, Michael Duckett, executive director of the agency overseeing the project, said Friday.

Duckett, who heads the state-created Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District, said the bill, if passed, could end up costing taxpayers more money by eliminating future financing options for the stadium and equipment.
"It would be like tying one hand behind our back," he said.
He said the district's board was committed to "protecting taxpayers" and did not need the constraints of the bill.

An aide to State Sen. Michael Ellis, R-Neenah, the Wisconsin Senate Republican Leader, said Thursday Ellis' bill, which is being drafted, would limit the district's financing particpation in the project to $160 million of bonds backed by a 0.1 percent, five-county sales tax.
Any cost overruns for the project would become the responsibility of the Brewers, the aide added.
Duckett said the bill did not formally come up at the district's board meeting Thursday in West Allis. He added that district officials were waiting to see the bill's language.
The board, however, did give the green light to the remarketing of $146.7 million of convertible option bonds into fixed-rate, long-term bonds in the next two weeks.
The bonds were rated A3 by Moody's Investors Service and A-minus by Standard & Poor's Corp.

Yaffa Rattner, a Moody's analyst, said Thursday the proposed legislation would not impact the rating on the bonds "given the fact the security of the bondholders is not married to the fortunes of the stadium."
Fred Haddad, a director at Standard & Poor's, also said the bill would not change the rating, but that the rating agency "would like to see the completion of the project not be threatened in anyway."
The district has a committment from MBIA Insurance Corp. to insure the bonds.
David Penchoff, a managing director at MBIA, said Friday that the insurer was comfortable that cost overruns would not pose any significant risk to the project.
